title_en: Mini-synthesis: three sources on green roofs
title_he: סינתזה קצרה: שלושה מקורות על גגות ירוקים

instructions.en: Argue whether the fictional town of Marrowby should require planted roofs on all new apartment buildings, and respond to opposing views, in a mini-synthesis of 350-500 words that draws on all three illustrative sources. Organise by idea, not source by source: show where the sources agree, conflict or qualify one another. Attribute every source-derived idea (author or organisation, year), paraphrase rather than patchwrite, quote only where the wording matters, and match the strength of each claim to the strength of its source. Say briefly how much weight each source deserves and why. Because the sources are fictional, you cannot check them laterally; instead, say in one sentence per source what you would check before relying on it in real research (who produced it and why, and what independent coverage says). Write your synthesis before you open the model, which answers a different question with different sources.

input_text:
All three sources are illustrative: they were invented for this task. The town, the authors, the council, the association and every figure are fictional and describe nothing in the real world.

Source A. Research summary. Ferrant, L., & Oyelaran, T. (2024). Planted roofs and summer indoor temperatures in Marrowby: a one-summer comparison. Marrowby Urban Review, 3(2), 14-29.

During one summer in the town of Marrowby, the researchers compared 12 apartment buildings with planted (green) roofs and 12 similar buildings with ordinary roofs. On the hottest days, top-floor apartments under planted roofs were on average 1.5 °C cooler in the afternoon than those under ordinary roofs. The difference was smaller on lower floors and almost disappeared on the ground floor. The authors note that the buildings were not randomly assigned, that the planted-roof buildings were on average newer, and that one summer may not be typical. They conclude that planted roofs "may help to reduce indoor heat on upper floors" and call for a study over several years.

Source B. Council briefing note. Marrowby Town Council, Planning Department (2025). Roof options for new apartment buildings.

The department estimates that a planted roof adds between 8% and 12% to the cost of building a roof, and that it needs an inspection twice a year, usually paid for by the residents' committee. Planted roofs hold back part of the rainwater in heavy storms, which can reduce flooding in the streets below. A white reflective coating costs far less; in a trial on two council buildings it lowered top-floor temperatures by about as much as the planted roofs in Source A, but it does nothing for rainwater. The note recommends that the council "consider a requirement for either option" and does not choose between them.

Source C. Opinion column. Marrowby Builders' Association newsletter (2025).

"Green roofs are an expensive fashion. Leaks are common, residents never want the maintenance bills, and buyers do not care what is on the roof. Any requirement will simply push up the price of new flats at a time when young families can barely afford one. The Association represents the town's building firms, and our members know what works."

scaffold.en: SIFT each source first: Stop; Investigate who produced it and why; Find other coverage; Trace claims back to their origin. Note one question per source.
Fill a synthesis grid: rows for ideas (cooling, cost and upkeep, rainwater, alternatives), columns for Sources A, B and C.
Plan by idea: thesis → first idea with the sources compared → second idea → strongest objection and rebuttal → conclusion.
Match reporting verbs to source strength: "found", "estimates", "reports", "asserts without evidence".

checklist.en: Claim: my position on the requirement is clear, and qualified if the evidence calls for it.
Synthesis: my paragraphs are organised by idea, not one per source, and show where the sources agree, conflict or qualify each other.
Source use: every source-derived idea is attributed and paraphrased in my own words and structure; I quote only where the wording matters.
Calibration: my claims are no stronger than their sources; small or interested sources get cautious reporting verbs.
Source weight: I say what kind of source each one is, how much weight it deserves, and what I would check laterally before relying on it.
Counterargument and rebuttal: I state the strongest opposing view fairly and answer it, and my conclusion adds nothing new.

model_answer:
Model for a parallel task: "Argue whether the fictional town of Kestwick should stop charging fines for overdue library books, and respond to opposing views", using three illustrative sources that were invented for this model (the town, the authors, the council, the forum and every figure are fictional). Source A: Halloran (2023), a one-year study of a fine-free trial at one of Kestwick's four branch libraries, which found that books came back slightly later on average but that 14% more lapsed members returned. Source B: a Kestwick Borough Council finance note (2024), which estimates that at two branches fines raise less than the staff time spent collecting them. Source C: a letter from the Kestwick Ratepayers' Forum (2024), which asserts that "without fines, nobody will bring books back". It answers a different question from yours, so study the moves, not the content.

Kestwick should replace overdue fines with reminders and loan limits, because the available evidence suggests that fines cost the library more in lost readers and staff time than they raise. The three sources deserve very different weight, however, and the case is stronger on finance than on borrowers' behaviour.

On income, the sources point the same way. Kestwick Borough Council (2024) estimates that at two of the town's four branches, fines raise less than it costs to collect them. A finance note has direct access to the library's accounts and no obvious stake in the outcome, so it deserves considerable weight, although its estimate covers only half the branches. Neither of the other sources offers figures on income.

On behaviour, the evidence is thinner and partly conflicting. Halloran (2023) reports that during a one-year trial at a single branch, books came back slightly later on average, while 14% more lapsed members returned. This suggests that removing fines may win back readers at a small cost in delays, but one branch over one year cannot show how the whole town would respond. The Ratepayers' Forum (2024) asserts that "without fines, nobody will bring books back". Halloran's finding contradicts this, and the letter cites no evidence, so it deserves little weight as a source of fact, although it may voice a concern that many residents share.

The strongest objection is that fines protect other readers rather than raise money: a borrower who keeps a book late keeps it from everyone else. This is a fair point, and Halloran's finding of slower returns supports it. Even so, the delay was small, and reminders, together with a limit on new loans for anyone with an overdue book, would protect other readers without shutting out borrowers who cannot pay. The proposal is therefore narrower than simple abolition: fines should be replaced, not merely removed.

Before relying on these sources in real research, I would check who funded Halloran's study and whether trials elsewhere found similar effects, whether anyone outside the council has reviewed its estimate, and whom the Ratepayers' Forum represents and what it has said about library spending before.

On balance, the evidence supports replacing fines with reminders and loan limits at all four branches, with the results reviewed against the council's figures after a year.

Moves: qualified thesis → idea 1 (income), sources compared and weighed → idea 2 (behaviour), sources in conflict and weighed → strongest objection, conceded in part, claim adjusted → what would be checked laterally, one point per source → conclusion with nothing new.
